title: So Close to Empire: The French in India, 1664-1954
sources: Rajiv Ahir, *A Brief History of Modern India*, ch. 3, "The French" and "The Anglo-French Struggle for Supremacy: the Carnatic Wars" (incl. "Causes for the English Success and the French Failure"; Dodwell; Lyall).

lines.text: How did France beat an army ten times its size, and still lose India?

lines.text: In seventeen forty-six, about a thousand French-led soldiers
beat an army of ten thousand in southern India.
lines.caps: *beat an army | of ten *thousand | in southern *India.

lines.text: Within a few years, a French governor was choosing

lines.text: who sat on India's thrones.
Yet in May seventeen sixty-six,
France executed its own general, the Kont duh Lally,
lines.caps: France *executed | its own *general, | the Comte de *Lally,

lines.text: for losing it all.
So what went wrong,
between almost winning and losing everything?
The answer wasn't a battle.
It was a supply line.
The French were the last Europeans to arrive,
so they had to move fast.
In sixteen sixty-four, King Louis the Fourteenth's ambitious minister, Kol-bair,
created the French East India Company,
with a fifty-year monopoly on France's eastern trade.
But it wasted its first years, and much of its money, on Madagascar.
lines.caps: But it *wasted | its first *years, | much of its *money, | on *Madagascar.

lines.text: So it turned to India.
In sixteen sixty-eight, François Ka-ron opened a factory at Surat,
and a year later, an Armenian merchant in French service, Mar-kaa-ra,
lines.caps: a year *later, | an *Armenian merchant | in French *service, | *Marcara,

lines.text: won trading rights from the Sultan of Golconda,
opening the way to Mussoo-lee-putnam.
The French had a foothold.
What they still lacked was a home.
That came in sixteen seventy-three,
when Shayr Khaan Lo-dee, a governor under the Sultan of Bee-jah-poor,
lines.caps: when *Sher Khan Lodi, | a *governor under | the Sultan of *Bijapur,

lines.text: granted them a site on the Coromandel coast.

lines.text: Pon-di-cherry grew there from sixteen seventy-four,
and François Martin turned it into the heart of French India.
lines.caps: François *Martin | *turned it into | the *heart | of *French India.

lines.text: But France's wars in Europe kept following it.
So in sixteen ninety-three, the Dutch captured Pon-di-cherry,
and only a peace treaty in Europe got it back.
So when the company was rebuilt in the seventeen-twenties,
lines.caps: So when the *company | was *rebuilt | in the *1720s,

lines.text: it built a safety net:
French islands in the Indian Ocean, Mauritius and Ray-oon-yon.
That safety net was about to become a weapon.
lines.caps: That *safety net | was about to *become | a *weapon.

lines.text: But in seventeen forty-six, Europe went to war again.
lines.caps: But in *1746, | Europe went to *war again.

lines.text: A French fleet from Mauritius, under La Boor-do-nay,
sailed to India and captured Madras from the English.
lines.caps: *sailed to India | and captured *Madras | from the *English.

lines.text: The French had promised Madras to the Nawab of the Carnatic.

lines.text: But they kept it,
so the Nawab sent an army to throw them out.

lines.text: At the Ud-yaar river, about a thousand French soldiers and trained sepoys

lines.text: faced some ten thousand men, and won.
Every European in India learned the same lesson:
a small, drilled army could beat a far bigger one.

lines.text: A treaty in Europe soon handed Madras back to the English.

lines.text: But one Frenchman had learned something bigger.
His name was Joseph François Doo-play,
and his idea was simple:
why conquer India's thrones,
when you can choose who sits on them?
lines.caps: when you can *choose | who *sits on them?

lines.text: So when rival princes fought over Hyderabad and the Carnatic,
lines.caps: So when rival *princes | fought over *Hyderabad | and the *Carnatic,

lines.text: Doo-play backed Moo-zaf-far Jung and Chun-da Saa-hib,
and the English backed their rivals.
So in seventeen forty-nine, at Aam-boor, Doo-play's side won,
and the Nawab Un-war-ood-deen was killed.
Therefore Doo-play was made governor of the Mughal lands south of the Krishna,
lines.caps: *Therefore Dupleix | was made *governor | of the *Mughal lands | south of the *Krishna,

lines.text: and a French army under Boo-see stayed at Hyderabad,
paid for by the ruler it protected.
It was a brilliant plan.
But the English had a young clerk who was watching closely.
lines.caps: But the *English had | a young *clerk | watching *closely.

lines.text: In seventeen fifty-one, that clerk, Robert Clive,
took the Carnatic capital, Aar-kot, with about five hundred men,
and held it through a fifty-two-day siege.
Therefore Doo-play's princes started losing.
So in seventeen fifty-two, Chun-da Saa-hib was captured and put to death.

lines.text: And back in Paris, the company's directors
were adding up the cost of Doo-play's wars.
So in seventeen fifty-four they called him home,
and his successor signed a truce with the English.
France had walked away from the board.
But the game was not over.
When the Seven Years War began,
France sent the Kont duh Lally, a proud and desperate general, to finish the English for good.
lines.caps: *France sent | the Comte de *Lally, | a proud, *desperate general, | to finish the *English | for *good.

lines.text: At first, he pushed them back toward Madras.

lines.text: But the English had something he didn't:
Bengal, won at Plassey,
sending them money, food and men.
Lally's supplies had to come the long way, overland.
So on the twenty-second of January, seventeen sixty,
at Won-dee-wosh, Sir Air Koot, patient and well supplied, defeated him decisively.
lines.caps: at *Wandiwash, | Sir Eyre *Coote, | patient and well *supplied, | defeated him *decisively.

lines.text: Lally retreated into Pon-di-cherry and held out for about eight months.

lines.text: Therefore, in January seventeen sixty-one, the city surrendered.
But France still needed someone to blame.
The Treaty of Paris, in seventeen sixty-three,
gave the French back their trading posts, but not their power.
lines.caps: gave the *French back | their trading *posts, | but not their *power.

lines.text: Clive himself said the English had done to the French

lines.text: exactly what the French had planned to do to them.

lines.text: Many historians call Plassey the turning point for British India.
lines.caps: Many historians call *Plassey | the *turning point | for British *India.

lines.text: But it was Won-dee-wosh that left the English with no European rival at all.

lines.text: So the blame fell on one man.
Lally went home a prisoner,
and five years later, France executed him.
But was the loss really his fault?
Yet the French never fully left.
Chun-der-na-gore joined India in nineteen fifty,
and Pon-di-cherry and the other French towns followed in nineteen fifty-four,
lines.caps: and *Pondicherry | and the other *French towns | followed in *1954,

lines.text: after a vote at Kee-zhoor.
So what really decided India?
France had the smartest idea:
rule through India's thrones, not around them.
But ideas need money,
and a company that waits for orders from Paris
can't outlast one that pays for itself from Bengal.
lines.caps: can't *outlast one | that pays for *itself | from *Bengal.

lines.text: The English took Doo-play's idea, added Bengal's money,
and built an empire with both.
